This game owes a lot-- like 98% of its mechanical and thematic structure-- to Uplink. It is mercifully less punishing than Uplink, though, a much more streamlined, modern experience. (Although, perhaps ironically, you'll do a lot more typing in Hacknet. Uplink's mostly mouse-driven UX feels weird and slow to me after a spending a few hours in Hacknet's terminal UX.) It isn't as robustly featured as its predecessor, but honestly I find the tidier structure refreshing.

If you enjoy Uplink but find it a little meandering, or you're tired of setting up bounce chains (which don't exist here), Hacknet will satisfy the same detail-oriented security puzzle-solving impulse.

So first and foremost: As someone who works with computer systems as a profession, I must admit that I am one of the few odd ones that really, *really* dislikes terminal based stuff. That being said, this game not only forced me to use the terminal, but actually gave me a reason to get used to using it, which has helped with my work. 

This game is enjoyable, extremely so. Going into this game with mixed feelings, especially with what I felt, at the time, was the most important plot element being spoiled (Bit's death) I wasn't really sure how to feel about it, but I quickly forgot all about that as I began tackling missions and getting used to the world. On my first day alone I clocked nearly 6 hours of game time, which is almost half of the time that I've spent on this game to date so far. I simply could not put it down. While it's not completely realistic, the concept is really well executed and it's definitely one of the more real hacking themed games that I've seen compared to others.

The game play starts off rather simple, and there isn't really much challenge in the beginning, but for those who aren't really computer savvy this gives them time to learn how to do some of the essentials while also testing their skills and improving. I think the first time I actually struggled was after getting counter-hacked by Naix and getting thrown into Terminal Mode, although I was freaking out over that because up until that point I had been really successful at avoiding any security in place; I was confused as I was positive that I had deleted everything in the logs dir and couldn't understand how I had been found. I wasn't aware that it was a scripted sequence until later. 

One thing I wish the game did a bit better though was when you failed to DC in time and were tracked. There was *so* much going on in the short amount of time you have to reset your IP that the first time it happened to me, I panicked and almost failed, resorting to closing out of the game (because what is cheating, right?). 

While there are a few issues with the game's missions, namely you being unable to complete missions if you've managed to wonder off to another one, overall I feel the game is extremely polished for something that started off as a small project. The missions are all enjoyable, the music is fantastic, the story is overall impressive (and the small logs scattered throughout the computers is a pretty enjoyable addition as well), and it just feels good as a whole. I haven't gotten around to playing the DLC yet, but if it's anything like the rest of the main game, I'm sure it won't disappoint in the slightest.

I would strongly recommend this to anyone who is looking for a bit of a more "realistic" hacking game. It makes you think, and teaches you some terminal basics, all while having fun in the process.

So after playing for a short while and considering my interest in cyber security, this game does really pull you into a different perspective altogether, especially if you're unaware of the concept behind malicious activities. This game puts you straight into the seat of a hacker, where cracking, executing and advanced computer knowledge is your weapon as you progress through the story in stages. At the start of the story, you begin in a tutorial stage which walks you through basic commands and how to hack a port and delete tracking information. As well as disconnecting from systems. The tutorial is well constructed and written, which helps the player understand what to do and how to do something to advance. The story also has no voice acting, but relies on text as if some anonymous user is contacting you - an example would be the in-game email system and intermissions. When it comes to presentation, it definitely makes you feel a part of something outside your comfort zone, as the hacking environment really does look and feel as if you're breaching unsecure or secured networks.

Overall, Hacknet doesn't fail to impress me and it's worth checking out if you're into cyber security or computer coding.

This game is... mediocre. The gameplay is monotonous and unchallenging, the storyline is fractured and uninspiring (it's even harder to take seriously since you're playing as a script kiddie), and the material is extremely far from reality.  As an actual Linux sysadmin, I am in particular annoyed by how poorly implemented common UNIX utilities are.  "ls *" and "rm ./*" fail, but "rm *" works? No "cp" or "mkdir"?  No way to delete directories? I can go on and on. Literally, I programmed more coreutils in a single college project than there are in this game. Couldn't they have just used busybox or something?  It certainly would have solved the issues the game has with file duplication in directories, since it'd be using actual files, rather than what is presumably a stack/queue/list/whatever.  And I would kill for io redirection.
Also, I'm mildly triggered by the executables being .exe files, but I'm definitely amused that you BSOD instead of kernel panicking.
I bought this game for a song, but I don't think I'd even recommend it if it were free, because in the time it takes you to play this game, you could have learned all sorts of actual UNIX commands in an actual terminal emulator on Linux, something that actually is free -- and you'd probably have a lot more fun, too.

Hacknet should not be a fun game. Usually, I despise games based off of dexterity, with a immense multitude of complicated mechanics and time limits.

But somehow, Hacknet pulls it off without a hitch. No matter how many missions I completed, the game never felt at all 'samey' or 'repetetive' and, whenever a time limit flashed up on my screen, I didn't groan with the realization that I would have to spend 2 days figuring out the exact combination of well-timed mouse clicks to move forward; I felt a sudden rush of adrenaline.

This is a game I never thought I'd fall in love with. 
This is a game I never thought I'd spend so much time on.
This is a game I never thought I'd be so invested in.
This is a game I never thought would be a long time favorite.

I could go on about how much I adore this game, but the fact of the matter is that you're looking at the reviews to gauge whether or not this is worth the buy. Am I wrong? Most likely not.

This is a game where you can feel like the badass hacker you've always wanted to be. Don't you dare lie to yourself and say that you've never wanted to be that shady figure in those movies or be like Sombra and hack the world. I promise you this game can fulfill that fantasy, and so much more.

In terms of gameplay, yes, it does get a bit repetitive, but every computer you crack and every puzzle you peice together is a completely new experience. 

Heck, while you're at it, go head and buy Labyrinths. It's literally a whole new game. With a whole new story line and new missions and computers and things to hack. Seriously. Do it.

And you know what? When you're done with all that, check out the Workshop! The modding community (We call ourselves Hacknet Extensions) are always pushing out new and fantastic stories and gameplay. If you really want to, you can join the Discord server and we can help you make your own (or just muck around and chat cuz we're nice people and sometimes coding gets tiring)

And hell, if you made it this far in this super long review, you might as well buy the game. It's worth it. I promise.

Hacknet is a fantastic hacking game with an interesting story. The interface is built around a set of simulated command line tools very close to the real Unix environment which is generally easy to use although the game map can get crowded in the late stages of the game. The atmosphere really does create the impression of being a hacker finding a target system's weaknesses, digging through your target's files and investigating what your contracts require. The gameplay rewards exploration and the game itself is peppered with lots of flourishes and attention to detail that really shows the love and effort put in by the developers. It recreates everything from private conversations to stupid corporate communications and IT practices (and even in-game OS crashes) realistically which makes for a very authentic game world.

While there are occasional typos and part of the gameplay loop migh seem repetitive, the flow of the game is very addictive and many times what starts off as a short session ends up taking up several hours. The game can definitely be enjoyed by non-computer savvy users although those with command-line experience are sure to find some amusing little touches that enhance the overall experience. The music and visuals are also very pleasant.

All in all, highly recommended and looking forward to playing the expansion!
